docs.title: Notes
docs.text: • Natural Language Processing (自然语言处理, 40470423-0) is a course taught by Tianxing He (贺天行) at Tsinghua University's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences (IIIS). These notes cover classical NLP, extensions to large language models, and selected research topics.

docs.title: Natural Language Processing
docs.text: Course notes based on Tianxing He's Natural Language Processing lectures at Tsinghua University's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences (IIIS).

docs.title: Course outline
docs.text:
1. Part 1 · Classical NLP covers grammars, statistical models, and word representations.
  2. Part 2 · LLM Extensions and Systems will cover language generation, reasoning, and efficient training and serving.
  3. Part 3 · Multimodality, Evaluation, and Agents will cover vision-language models, generated-text detection, evaluation, and agents.

docs.title: Part 1 · Classical NLP
docs.text: Part 1 starts with explicit rules for sentence structure and then moves on to statistical models of text and learned word representations.

docs.title: Why study classical NLP?
docs.text: Comparing classical models with large language models (LLMs) shows how NLP has changed and highlights the simplicity of classical approaches. Classical models can be much faster for specific tasks. For example, an n-gram language model can look up a next-token probability in a table.

docs.title: The correct mindset
docs.text:
Human language looks to a machine the way an alien language looks to us. Imagine receiving a transmission that starts with f84hh4zl8da4dzwrzo40hiz…. You can see the characters. You have to infer where the words begin, how they combine, and what they mean.

  1. Find patterns in the characters. Count which characters follow each symbol and use conditional entropy to measure how uncertain the next character is. In the alien sample, the next character is especially hard to predict after z.
  2. Test a word boundary. A separator could explain that uncertainty because many different words can follow it. Splitting on z reveals repeated chunks such as j74. The chunks r9xv and r9yx both occur between 5hec and j7hek67, so they may play similar roles.
  3. Connect the text to observations. Show the alien a picture of a spacecraft and a picture of an alien. Both replies contain r99t. The alien holds up two tentacles for the spacecraft and one for the alien. More examples pairing text with pictures and counts would let you test what the recurring chunks mean.

This is the perspective we take in classical NLP. We start with observable patterns, use them to make hypotheses about language, and test those hypotheses against more data.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. Learn production rules, parse trees, and CKY parsing in Context-free grammars.
  2. Latent semantic analysis uses term-document matrices and singular value decomposition to represent words and documents.
  3. Gaussian mixture models and expectation-maximization introduce learning with hidden variables.
  4. Hidden Markov models support inference and learning for sequence tasks such as part-of-speech tagging.
  5. N-gram language models estimate token probabilities from a short context.
  6. Word2vec learns embeddings by predicting a word from its context or by predicting context words from a target word.
  7. Directed graphical models generalize the conditional independence ideas introduced by HMMs.

docs.title: Context-free grammars
docs.text: Modern LLM user neural networks to do "blackbox" generation, while CFG can give you "whitebox" generation, etc., through a parse tree.

docs.title: Productions and derivations
docs.text:
A context-free grammar (CFG) is a tuple \(G = (N, \Sigma, P, S)\) where

  • \(N\) is a finite set of nonterminals, the symbols that rules can rewrite.
  • \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of terminals, the symbols that make up the generated strings. The sets \(N\) and \(\Sigma\) are disjoint.
  • \(P \subseteq N \times (N \cup \Sigma)^*\) is a finite set of productions. We write \((A, \alpha) \in P\) as \(A \rightarrow \alpha\). The right-hand side \(\alpha\) can be the empty string \(\epsilon\).
  • \(S \in N\) is the start symbol.

For each production \(A \rightarrow \alpha\) and any surrounding strings \(u, v \in (N \cup \Sigma)^*\), the grammar permits the rewrite

\[ uAv \Rightarrow_G u\alpha v. \]

The grammar is context-free because the rule can rewrite \(A\) regardless of its context \(u\) and \(v\). The arrow \(\rightarrow\) specifies a production, \(\Rightarrow_G\) denotes one rewrite step, and \(\Rightarrow_G^*\) denotes zero or more steps.

The language generated by \(G\) is

\[ \mathcal{L}(G) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid S \Rightarrow_G^* w\}. \]

A language \(L\) is context-free if \(L = \mathcal{L}(G)\) for some CFG \(G\).

docs.title: Arithmetic expressions
docs.text:
Let \(E\) be the start symbol and \(N = \{E, \mathrm{Op}\}\). The terminal set is

\[ \Sigma = \{\mathtt{int}, \mathtt{+}, \mathtt{*}, \mathtt{-}, \mathtt{/}, \mathtt{(}, \mathtt{)}\}, \]

where \(\mathtt{int}\) is a single terminal token. The productions are

\[ \begin{aligned} E &\rightarrow E\,\mathrm{Op}\,E \mid \mathtt{int} \mid \mathtt{(}E\mathtt{)}, \\ \mathrm{Op} &\rightarrow \mathtt{+} \mid \mathtt{*} \mid \mathtt{-} \mid \mathtt{/}. \end{aligned} \]

Each step in the following derivation rewrites one occurrence of a nonterminal.

\[ \begin{aligned} & E \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& E\,\mathrm{Op}\,E \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& E\,\mathrm{Op}\,\mathtt{(}E\mathtt{)} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& E\,\mathrm{Op}\,\mathtt{(}E\,\mathrm{Op}\,E\mathtt{)} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& E\mathtt{*(}E\,\mathrm{Op}\,E\mathtt{)} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& \mathtt{int*(}E\,\mathrm{Op}\,E\mathtt{)} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& \mathtt{int*(int}\,\mathrm{Op}\,E\mathtt{)} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& \mathtt{int*(int}\,\mathrm{Op}\,\mathtt{int)} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;& \mathtt{int*(int+int)}. \end{aligned} \]

The final string contains only terminals, so \(\mathtt{int*(int+int)} \in \mathcal{L}(G)\).

docs.title: A non-context-free language
docs.text:
Let \(L = \{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \ge 1\}\). The three blocks occur in order and have the same length. No CFG generates \(L\). See Wikipedia’s pumping-lemma proof.

A grammar \(H\) that generates \(L\) has start symbol \(S\). Its nonterminals are \(\{S, B, C\}\) and its terminals are \(\{a, b, c\}\). The productions are

\[ \begin{alignedat}{2} S &\rightarrow aSBC \mid aBC, \\ CB &\rightarrow BC, \\ aB &\rightarrow ab, & \quad bB &\rightarrow bb, \\ bC &\rightarrow bc, & \quad cC &\rightarrow cc. \end{alignedat} \]

The rule \(CB \rightarrow BC\) can apply only when \(C\) is immediately followed by \(B\). This violates the CFG definition, which requires a single nonterminal on the left-hand side of each production.

docs.title: Converting a regular expression to a CFG
docs.text:
The regular expression ab*[cde] matches strings of the form \(ab^k t\) for \(k \ge 0\) and \(t \in \{c, d, e\}\). An equivalent CFG has start symbol \(S\) and productions

\[ S \rightarrow aBC, \allowbreak\quad B \rightarrow bB \mid \epsilon, \allowbreak\quad C \rightarrow c \mid d \mid e. \]

docs.title: A CFG with no equivalent regular expression
docs.text:
The CFG with start symbol \(S\) and productions

\[ S \rightarrow aSb \mid ab \]

generates \(L = \{a^n b^n \mid n \ge 1\}\).

The language \(L\) is nonregular, so no formal regular expression describes it. The pumping-lemma argument works for both \(n \ge 0\) and \(n \ge 1\). See Wikipedia’s worked example.

docs.title: A small English grammar
docs.text:
The following productions describe a fragment of English called \(L_0\). The categories \(\mathrm{NP}\), \(\mathrm{VP}\), and \(\mathrm{PP}\) denote noun phrases, verb phrases, and prepositional phrases. In the rules and the tree below, \(\mathrm{Pro}\) stands for pronoun, \(\mathrm{Det}\) for determiner, and \(\mathrm{Nom}\) for nominal.

\[ \begin{aligned} S &\rightarrow \mathrm{NP}\,\mathrm{VP}, \\ \mathrm{NP} &\rightarrow \mathrm{Pro} \mid \text{Proper-Noun} \goodbreak \mid \mathrm{Det}\,\mathrm{Nom}, \\ \mathrm{Nom} &\rightarrow \mathrm{Nom}\,\mathrm{Noun} \mid \mathrm{Noun}, \\ \mathrm{VP} &\rightarrow \mathrm{Verb} \mid \mathrm{Verb}\,\mathrm{NP} \goodbreak \mid \mathrm{Verb}\,\mathrm{NP}\,\mathrm{PP}, \\ \mathrm{PP} &\rightarrow \mathrm{Preposition}\,\mathrm{NP}. \end{aligned} \]

The parse tree for “I prefer a morning flight” shows how the words form a noun phrase and a verb phrase.

The grammar captures phrase structure and can also license implausible combinations. For example, \(\mathrm{VP} \rightarrow \mathrm{Verb}\,\mathrm{NP}\) allows both “prefer a flight” and “write a flight” if both verbs have the same lexical category.

docs.title: Chomsky normal form
docs.text:
A CFG \(G = (N, \Sigma, P, S)\) is in Chomsky normal form (CNF) if its productions have one of two forms.

\[ \begin{alignedat}{2} A &\rightarrow BC, & \quad &A,B,C \in N, \\ A &\rightarrow a, & \quad &A \in N,\ a \in \Sigma. \end{alignedat} \]

With these rules, every generated string is nonempty, so \(\mathcal{L}(G) \subseteq \Sigma^+\). For any CFG \(G\), there is a grammar in this form that generates \(\mathcal{L}(G) \setminus \{\epsilon\}\). To preserve \(\epsilon\) when it belongs to the language, the extended form also allows \(S \rightarrow \epsilon\), provided \(S\) never appears on a right-hand side.

docs.title: Converting a rule to CNF
docs.text:
CFG:

\[ A \rightarrow BCD. \]

CNF:

\[ A \rightarrow BX, \qquad X \rightarrow CD. \]

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
Syntactic parsing finds the parse trees a grammar assigns to a sentence. The Cocke–Kasami–Younger (CKY) algorithm uses dynamic programming to combine shorter spans into longer ones.

First convert the grammar to CNF. For a nonempty input \(w_1 \cdots w_n\), let \(T[i,j]\) store the nonterminals \(A \in N\) that derive the span \((i,j]\), where \(0 \le i < j \le n\).

\[ T[i,j] = \{A \mid A \Rightarrow_G^* w_{i+1}\cdots w_j\}. \]

Fill the one-token spans \(T[i, i+1]\) using terminal productions. For each longer span, try every split point \(k\) and use binary productions to combine the two subspans.

\[ \begin{array}{@{}l@{}} T[i,j] \gets \varnothing \quad (0 \le i < j \le n) \\ \mathbf{for}\ j \gets 1\ \mathbf{to}\ n\ \mathbf{do} \\ \enspace T[j-1,j] \gets \{A \mid (A \rightarrow w_j) \in P\} \\ \enspace \mathbf{for}\ i \gets j-2\ \mathbf{downto}\ 0\ \mathbf{do} \\ \quad \mathbf{for}\ k \gets i+1\ \mathbf{to}\ j-1\ \mathbf{do} \\ \quad\enspace \textbf{for each}\ (A \rightarrow BC) \in P \\ \qquad \mathbf{if}\ B \in T[i,k] \land C \in T[k,j] \\ \qquad\enspace T[i,j] \gets T[i,j] \cup \{A\} \\ \mathbf{return}\ T \end{array} \]

The input belongs to \(\mathcal{L}(G)\) exactly when \(S \in T[0,n]\). To recover parse trees, also record the productions and split points that added each nonterminal to the chart.

A sentence can have multiple parses. In “I shot an elephant in my pajamas,” the phrase “in my pajamas” can attach to the noun phrase “an elephant” or to the verb phrase “shot an elephant.” A probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) assigns probabilities to productions, which can be estimated from annotated data. A parse tree's probability is the product of the probabilities of its productions, so a parser can rank competing trees.

docs.title: Synchronous context-free grammars
docs.text:
A synchronous context-free grammar (S-CFG) with a shared nonterminal set is a tuple

\[ G = (N, \Sigma_{\mathrm{src}}, \Sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}, P, S). \]

Here \(N\) is a finite set of nonterminals, \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{src}}\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}\) are finite source and target terminal alphabets disjoint from \(N\), \(S \in N\) is the start symbol, and \(P\) is a finite set of productions.

For a string \(\gamma\), let \(I_N(\gamma)\) be its set of nonterminal positions.

\[ I_N(\gamma) = \{i \mid 1 \le i \le |\gamma|,\ \gamma_i \in N\}. \]

A production has the form \(A \rightarrow \langle \alpha, \beta, \pi \rangle\), where \(A \in N\) and the two strings are drawn from their respective alphabets.

\[ \alpha \in (N \cup \Sigma_{\mathrm{src}})^*, \allowbreak\quad \beta \in (N \cup \Sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}})^*. \]

The bijection \(\pi \colon I_N(\alpha) \to I_N(\beta)\) links occurrences of the same nonterminal, so \(\alpha_i = \beta_{\pi(i)}\) for every \(i \in I_N(\alpha)\). Matching subscripts mark linked occurrences.

A rewrite applies one production to both occurrences of a linked nonterminal \(A_k\).

\[ \langle u A_k v,\ u' A_k v' \rangle \Rightarrow_G \langle u\widetilde{\alpha}v,\ u'\widetilde{\beta}v' \rangle, \]

where \(\widetilde{\alpha}\) and \(\widetilde{\beta}\) are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with a fresh shared subscript for each pair \((i, \pi(i))\). The grammar generates the relation

\[ \mathcal{L}(G) = \bigl\{(x,y) \in \Sigma_{\mathrm{src}}^* \times \Sigma_{\mathrm{tgt}}^* \bigm| \allowbreak \langle S_0,S_0\rangle \Rightarrow_G^* \langle x,y\rangle\bigr\}. \]

docs.title: English–Japanese example
docs.text:
The first component of each pair is English, and the second is romanized Japanese.

\[ \begin{aligned} S &\rightarrow \langle \mathrm{NP}_1\,\mathrm{VP}_2,\ \mathrm{NP}_1\,\mathrm{VP}_2\rangle, \\ \mathrm{VP} &\rightarrow \langle \mathrm{V}_1\,\mathrm{NP}_2,\ \mathrm{NP}_2\,\mathrm{V}_1\rangle, \\ \mathrm{NP} &\rightarrow \langle \text{I},\ \text{watashi wa}\rangle \goodbreak \mid \langle \text{the box},\ \text{hako wo}\rangle, \\ \mathrm{V} &\rightarrow \langle \text{open},\ \text{akemasu}\rangle. \end{aligned} \]

The \(\mathrm{VP}\) rule places the object after the verb in English and before it in Japanese.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\langle S_0,S_0\rangle \\ \Rightarrow_G\;&\langle \mathrm{NP}_1\,\mathrm{VP}_2,\ \mathrm{NP}_1\,\mathrm{VP}_2\rangle \\ \Rightarrow_G\;&\langle \text{I}\ \mathrm{VP}_2,\ \text{watashi wa}\ \mathrm{VP}_2\rangle \\ \Rightarrow_G\;&\begin{indentalign}[0em]{l} \langle \text{I}\ \mathrm{V}_3\,\mathrm{NP}_4, \goodbreak\ \text{watashi~wa}\ \mathrm{NP}_4\,\mathrm{V}_3\rangle \end{indentalign} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;&\begin{indentalign}[0em]{l} \langle \text{I open}\ \mathrm{NP}_4, \goodbreak\ \text{watashi~wa}\ \mathrm{NP}_4\ \text{akemasu}\rangle \end{indentalign} \\ \Rightarrow_G\;&\begin{indentalign}[0em]{l} \langle \text{I open the box}, \goodbreak\ \text{watashi~wa hako~wo akemasu}\rangle. \end{indentalign} \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Hidden Markov models
docs.text: We will mainly follow Chapter 5, “Inference for Markov Models,” from Random Processes for Engineers, adding examples from the lecture slides.

docs.title: Basics of estimation theory
docs.text: What is estimation? Suppose a parameter \(\theta\) is to be estimated from a random variable \(Y\). An estimator of \(\theta\) is a function \(\hat{\theta}\) that gives the estimate \(\hat{\theta}(y)\) for each observed value \(y\).

docs.title: Two views: ML and Bayes
docs.text:
Definition 1 (maximum likelihood). Suppose the distribution of \(Y\) is known for each admissible parameter \(\theta\). Fix the observed value \(y\). Its likelihood as a function of \(\theta\) and the corresponding maximum likelihood (ML) estimate are

\[ L(\theta;y)= \begin{cases} p_Y(y\mid\theta), & Y \text{ discrete},\\ f_Y(y\mid\theta), & Y \text{ continuous}, \end{cases} \qquad \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{ML}}(y)\in\arg\max_{\theta} L(\theta;y). \tag{1} \]

ML can impose hard constraints by restricting the admissible values of \(\theta\). A Bayesian model can also express prior beliefs by giving the unknown quantity a probability distribution.

Definition 2 (Bayes estimator). Let \(Z\) be the quantity to estimate and \(Y\) the observation, with a known joint distribution. Let \(C(z,\hat z)\) be the cost of reporting \(\hat z\) when the true value is \(z\). A Bayes estimator \(\hat Z=g^*(Y)\) minimizes the average cost over estimation rules \(g\):

\[ g^*\in\arg\min_g \mathbb E \left[C\left(Z,g(Y)\right)\right]. \tag{2} \]

The prior is the distribution of \(Z\) before observing \(Y\). The posterior is the conditional distribution of \(Z\) given \(Y=y\). For discrete \(Z\), their probability mass functions are \(p_Z(z)\) and \(p_{Z\mid Y}(z\mid y)\). For jointly continuous \(Z,Y\), their densities are \(f_Z(z)\) and \(f_{Z\mid Y}(z\mid y)\).

docs.title: MMSE and MAP estimators
docs.text:
Under squared-error loss, the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate is the posterior mean:

\[ C(z,\hat z)=(z-\hat z)^2,\qquad \hat Z_{\mathrm{MMSE}}(y)=\mathbb E[Z\mid Y=y]. \tag{3} \]

For discrete \(Z\), zero-one loss \(C(z,\hat z)=\mathbf 1_{\{z\ne\hat z\}}\) assigns unit cost to an incorrect estimate. Given \(Y=y\), reporting \(z\) has expected cost \(1-p_{Z\mid Y}(z\mid y)\). Minimizing this cost gives the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate:

\[ \hat Z_{\mathrm{MAP}}(y)\in\arg\max_z p_{Z\mid Y}(z\mid y). \tag{4} \]

Returning to the parameter notation, let \(\Theta\) and \(Y\) be discrete random variables. For an observation with \(p_Y(y)>0\), Bayes' rule gives

\[ p_{\Theta\mid Y}(\theta\mid y) =\frac{p_\Theta(\theta)\,p_Y(y\mid\theta)}{p_Y(y)}, \qquad p_Y(y)=\sum_{\theta'}p_\Theta(\theta')\,p_Y(y\mid\theta'). \tag{5} \]

Here \(p_Y(y\mid\theta)\) denotes the likelihood under \(\Theta=\theta\). With \(y\) fixed, the denominator \(p_Y(y)\) is constant across candidate values of \(\theta\), so (5) gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat\Theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}(y) &\in\arg\max_\theta p_{\Theta\mid Y}(\theta\mid y)\\ &=\arg\max_\theta \frac{p_\Theta(\theta)\,p_Y(y\mid\theta)}{p_Y(y)}\\ &=\arg\max_\theta p_\Theta(\theta)\,p_Y(y\mid\theta). \end{aligned} \tag{6} \]

Recall that the maximum likelihood estimate satisfies

\[ \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{ML}}(y)\in\arg\max_{\theta} p_Y(y\mid\theta). \tag{7} \]

If the prior is uniform over the admissible parameter values, its factor is constant too. MAP and ML then have the same maximizers.

For jointly continuous \(\Theta\) and \(Y\), the MAP estimate maximizes the posterior density:

\[ \hat\Theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}(y) \in\arg\max_\theta f_{\Theta\mid Y}(\theta\mid y) =\arg\max_\theta f_\Theta(\theta)\,f_Y(y\mid\theta). \tag{8} \]

docs.title: The expectation-maximization algorithm
docs.text:
The expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative method for maximum-likelihood estimation in models with latent variables.

Notation.

  • \(\theta\) is the parameter to estimate. \(\theta^{(k)}\) is its value at iteration \(k\).
  • \(X\) is the complete data. Its probability mass function \(p_{\mathrm{cd}}(x\mid\theta)\) is specified for each \(\theta\).
  • \(Y=h(X)\) is the observed random vector, and \(y\) is its observed value. Write \(\mathcal F_y=\{x:h(x)=y\}\) for all complete-data values consistent with \(y\).
  • When \(X=(Y,Z)\), \(Z\) denotes the unobserved component. In this case \(h(y,z)=y\), so summing over \(\mathcal F_y\) amounts to summing over \(z\) with \(y\) fixed.

The observed-data likelihood is the total probability of the complete-data values that yield \(y\):

\[ p(y\mid\theta)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal F_y}p_{\mathrm{cd}}(x\mid\theta). \tag{9} \]

In some applications, there can be a very large number of terms in (9), making direct numerical maximization of \(p(y\mid \theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\) computationally infeasible (i.e., infeasible to compute \(\hat{\theta}_{\text{ML}}(y)\)).

docs.title: Algorithm: Expectation-maximization
docs.text:
An observation \(y\) is given, along with an initial estimate \(\theta^{(0)}\).

(Expectation step) Compute \(Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(k)})\) for all \(\theta\), where

\[ Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(k)})=\mathbb E\!\left[\log p_{\mathrm{cd}}(X\mid\theta)\mid y,\theta^{(k)}\right]. \tag{10} \]

(Maximization step) Compute \(\theta^{(k+1)}\in\arg\max_{\theta} Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(k)})\).

A common source of confusion is the different roles of \(\theta\) and \(\theta^{(k)}\): the posterior weights are computed using \(\theta^{(k)}\), while the complete-data log-likelihood is evaluated at \(\theta\).

\[ \begin{aligned} Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(k)}) =\sum_{x\in\mathcal F_y} \frac{p_{\mathrm{cd}}(x\mid\theta^{(k)})}{p(y\mid\theta^{(k)})} \log p_{\mathrm{cd}}(x\mid\theta), \qquad p(y\mid\theta^{(k)})>0. \end{aligned} \tag{11} \]

docs.title: Convergence of the EM algorithm
docs.text:
Suppose that the complete data pmf can be factored as

\[ p_{X, Y}(x, y\mid \theta) = p_{\text{cd}}(x\mid \theta) \mathbf{1}_{\{h(x)=y\}}=p(y\mid \theta)k(x\mid y, \theta) \tag{12} \]

Assume the following conditions hold:

  1. The map \(\theta\mapsto\log p(y\mid\theta)\) is differentiable.
  2. For every \(\bar\theta\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb E[\log k(X\mid y,\bar\theta)\mid y,\bar\theta]\) is finite.
  3. For each fixed \(\theta\), the map \(\theta'\mapsto D\!\left(k(\cdot\mid y,\theta)\,\|\,k(\cdot\mid y,\theta')\right)\) is differentiable.
  4. For each fixed \(\theta'\), the map \(\theta\mapsto D\!\left(k(\cdot\mid y,\theta)\,\|\,k(\cdot\mid y,\theta')\right)\) is continuous.

If \(p(y\mid\theta^{(0)})>0\), the EM iterates satisfy \(p(y\mid\theta^{(k+1)})\ge p(y\mid\theta^{(k)})\) for every \(k\). Every limit point \(\theta^*\) of the parameter sequence is stationary for the likelihood:

\[ \left.\nabla_\theta p(y\mid\theta)\right|_{\theta=\theta^*}=0. \tag{13} \]

Here we only prove the nondecreasing part. Using the factorization

\[ p_{\text{cd}}(x\mid \theta)=p(y\mid \theta) k(x \mid y, \theta) \tag{14} \]

for \(x \in \mathcal{F}_{y}\),

\[ \begin{aligned} Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(k)}) &=\mathbb E\!\left[\log p_{\mathrm{cd}}(X\mid\theta)\,\middle|\,y,\theta^{(k)}\right]\\ &=\log p(y\mid\theta) +\mathbb E\!\left[\log k(X\mid y,\theta)\,\middle|\,y,\theta^{(k)}\right]\\ &=\log p(y\mid\theta) +\mathbb E\!\left[\log\frac{k(X\mid y,\theta)}{k(X\mid y,\theta^{(k)})}\,\middle|\,y,\theta^{(k)}\right]+\mathbb E\!\left[\log k(X\mid y,\theta^{(k)})\,\middle|\,y,\theta^{(k)}\right]\\ &=\log p(y\mid\theta) -D\!\left(k(\cdot\mid y,\theta^{(k)})\,\|\,k(\cdot\mid y,\theta)\right)+\mathbb E\!\left[\log k(X\mid y,\theta^{(k)})\,\middle|\,y,\theta^{(k)}\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{15} \]

Notice that the last term \(\mathbb{E}\left[\log k(X \mid y, \theta^{(k)}) \middle| y, \theta^{(k)} \right]\) is constant with respect to \(\theta\). The maximization step is equivalent to:

\[ \theta^{(k+1)} = \arg \max_{\theta} \left[ \log p(y \mid \theta) - D \left( k(\cdot \mid y, \theta^{(k)} ) \| k(\cdot \mid y, \theta) \right) \right]. \tag{16} \]

Therefore,

\[ \log p(y\mid \theta^{(k+1)}) - D\left( k(\cdot \mid y, \theta^{(k)})\| k(\cdot \mid y, \theta^{(k+1)}) \right) \geq \log p(y \mid \theta^{(k)}) - D \left( k(\cdot \mid y, \theta^{(k)}) \| k(\cdot \mid y, \theta^{(k)}) \right) = \log p(y \mid \theta^{(k)}). \tag{17} \]

docs.title: Example: Gaussian mixture model
docs.text:
An observed random vector \(Y\in\mathbb R^d\) follows a mixture of \(J\) Gaussian distributions. Let \(Z\in\{1,\ldots,J\}\) be the unobserved component label. The parameter is \( heta=(\pi,\mu,\Sigma)\), where

  • \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_J)\) contains the mixing weights. \(\pi_j=P(Z=j)\)
  • \(\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_J)\) contains the component means. \(\mu_j=\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=j]\in\mathbb R^d\).
  • \(\Sigma=(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_J)\) contains the component covariance matrices. \(\Sigma_j=\operatorname{Cov}(Y\mid Z=j) \in \mathbb{R}^{d imes d}.\)

Thus \(Y\mid Z=j\sim\mathcal N(\mu_j,\Sigma_j), Z \sim ext{Categorical}(\pi)\). Next, we derive the EM algorithm steps in an attempt to compute the maximum likelihood estimate of \( heta\) given independent observations \(y^{(1)}, y^{(2)}, \dots, y^{(n)}\).

Let \(X = (Z^{(1)}, Y^{(1)}, Z^{(2)}, Y^{(2)}, \dots, Z^{(n)}, Y^{(n)})\). Then we have

\[ egin{aligned} p_{\mathrm{cd}}(X\mid heta)&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{Z^{(i)}}\,\mathcal N\!\left(Y^{(i)}\mid\mu_{Z^{(i)}},\Sigma_{Z^{(i)}} ight) \ &= \prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{j=1}^J \left( \pi_{j} \mathcal{N} \left( Y^{(i)} \mid \mu_{j}, \Sigma_{j} ight) ight) ^{\mathbf{1}\{Z^{(i)}=j\}}. \end{aligned} ag{18} \]

For \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and \(j=1,\ldots,J\), define:

\[ egin{aligned} r_{ij}^{(k)} &=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\{Z^{(i)}=j\}}\,\middle|\,Y^{(1)}=y^{(1)},\ldots,Y^{(n)}=y^{(n)}, heta^{(k)} ight]\ &=P\!\left(Z^{(i)}=j\mid Y^{(i)}=y^{(i)}, heta^{(k)} ight)\ &= rac{\pi_j^{(k)}\,\mathcal N\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid\mu_j^{(k)},\Sigma_j^{(k)} ight)} {\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\pi_\ell^{(k)}\,\mathcal N\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid\mu_\ell^{(k)},\Sigma_\ell^{(k)} ight)}. \end{aligned} ag{19} \]

Let \(y=(y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(n)})\) denote the observed sample. Only the component indicators are random:

\[ egin{aligned} Q( heta\mid heta^{(k)}) &=\mathbb E\!\left[\log p_{\mathrm{cd}}(X\mid heta)\,\middle|\,y, heta^{(k)} ight]\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{J} \mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\{Z^{(i)}=j\}}\,\middle|\,y, heta^{(k)} ight] \log\!\left[\pi_j\,\mathcal N\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j ight) ight]\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{J}r_{ij}^{(k)} \left[\log\pi_j+\log\mathcal N\!\left(y^{(i)}\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j ight) ight]. \end{aligned} ag{20} \]

Keep track of what is being conditioned on and which variables the expectation is taken over. Confusing the two can lead to incorrect updates and make the optimization unnecessarily difficult.

In the M-step,

\[ egin{aligned} \arg\max_{ heta} Q( heta\mid heta^{(k)}) &=\arg\max_{\pi,\mu,\Sigma} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{J} r_{ij}^{(k)} \left[ \log\pi_j- rac12\log\det\Sigma_j - rac12(y^{(i)}-\mu_j)^ op\Sigma_j^{-1}(y^{(i)}-\mu_j) ight]. \end{aligned} ag{21} \]

Both maximizations use the GMM constraints \(\pi_j\ge 0\), \(\sum_{j=1}^{J}\pi_j=1\), and \(\Sigma_j\succ 0\) for each component.

  • Mixing weights update

    \[ oxed{\pi_j^{(k+1)}= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)}.} ag{22} \]
Matrix Cookbook identities used below

For fixed vectors \(a,b\) and matrix \(B\), the vector and matrix gradients are

\[ egin{aligned} abla_x(x^ op Bx)&=(B+B^ op)x && ext{(81)},\ abla_X\log|\det X|&=X^{- op} && ext{(57)},\ abla_X(a^ op X^{-1}b)&=-X^{- op}ab^ op X^{- op} && ext{(61)}. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(X^{- op}=(X^{-1})^ op\). For a positive-definite covariance matrix, \(\Sigma_j^{- op}=\Sigma_j^{-1}\). Petersen and Pedersen, The Matrix Cookbook, 2012, pp. 9–11

  • Mean update

    \[ abla_{\mu_j}Q =\Sigma_j^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)}(y^{(i)}-\mu_j). ag{23} \]

    Set this gradient to zero and multiply by \(\Sigma_j\).

    \[ oxed{\mu_j^{(k+1)}= rac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)}y^{(i)}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)}}.} ag{24} \]

  • Covariance update

    \[ abla_{\Sigma_j}Q =- rac12\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)} ight)\Sigma_j^{-1} + rac12\Sigma_j^{-1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)}(y^{(i)}-\mu_j^{(k+1)})(y^{(i)}-\mu_j^{(k+1)})^ op ight)\Sigma_j^{-1}. ag{25} \]

    Set the gradient to zero and multiply on both the left and the right by \(\Sigma_j\).

    \[ oxed{\Sigma_j^{(k+1)} = rac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)} (y^{(i)}-\mu_j^{(k+1)})(y^{(i)}-\mu_j^{(k+1)})^ op} {\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{ij}^{(k)}}.} ag{26} \]

docs.title: NumPy implementation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from numpy.typing import NDArray

FloatArray = NDArray[np.float64]


def gmm_em(
    Y: FloatArray,                  # (n, d)
    pi_init: FloatArray,            # (J,)
    mu_init: FloatArray,            # (J, d)
    sigma_init: FloatArray,         # (J, d, d)
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float | None = None,
    reg_covar: float = 0.0,
) -> tuple[FloatArray, FloatArray, FloatArray, FloatArray, FloatArray]:
    """Fit a full-covariance GMM using EM.

    tol=None runs exactly max_iter iterations. Otherwise, stop when
    the absolute change in total observed-data log-likelihood is < tol.
    max_iter must be nonnegative; tol, if supplied, must be positive;
    reg_covar must be nonnegative.

    Returns:
        pi:     (J,) mixing weights.
        mu:     (J, d) means.
        Sigma:  (J, d, d) covariances.
        r:      (n, J) responsibilities under the returned parameters.
        loglik: (t + 1,) log-likelihoods, including initialization,
                where t is the number of completed EM iterations.
    """
    n, d = Y.shape
    J = pi_init.shape[0]
    pi = np.array(pi_init, dtype=np.float64, copy=True)       # (J,)
    mu = np.array(mu_init, dtype=np.float64, copy=True)       # (J, d)
    Sigma = np.array(sigma_init, dtype=np.float64, copy=True) # (J, d, d)
    eye = np.eye(d, dtype=np.float64)                         # (d, d)

    def e_step(
        weights: FloatArray,    # (J,)
        means: FloatArray,      # (J, d)
        covs: FloatArray,       # (J, d, d)
    ) -> tuple[FloatArray, float]:
        log_joint = np.empty((n, J), dtype=np.float64)  # (n, J)
        for j in range(J):
            L = np.linalg.cholesky(covs[j])            # (d, d)
            diff = Y - means[j]                       # (n, d)
            z = np.linalg.solve(L, diff.T)             # (d, n)
            mahal = np.sum(z * z, axis=0)              # (n,)
            log_det = 2.0 * np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
            log_joint[:, j] = np.log(weights[j]) - 0.5 * (
                d * np.log(2.0 * np.pi) + log_det + mahal
            )

        # Stable log(sum_j pi_j * N(y_i | mu_j, Sigma_j)).
        shift = log_joint.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # (n, 1)
        log_density = shift + np.log(
            np.exp(log_joint - shift).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        )                                                     # (n, 1)
        responsibilities = np.exp(log_joint - log_density)     # (n, J)
        return responsibilities, float(log_density.sum())

    r, ll = e_step(pi, mu, Sigma)
    history: list[float] = [ll]

    for _ in range(max_iter):
        # M-step: keep r fixed throughout all three updates.
        counts = r.sum(axis=0)                       # (J,)
        pi = counts / n                             # (J,)
        mu = (r.T @ Y) / counts[:, None]             # (J, d)
        diff = Y[None, :, :] - mu[:, None, :]        # (J, n, d)
        Sigma = np.einsum(
            "jn,jnd,jne->jde", r.T, diff, diff
        ) / counts[:, None, None]                   # (J, d, d)
        Sigma += reg_covar * eye                     # (J, d, d)

        # E-step under the updated parameters.
        r, ll = e_step(pi, mu, Sigma)
        history.append(ll)
        if tol is not None and abs(history[-1] - history[-2]) < tol:
            break

    loglik = np.asarray(history, dtype=np.float64)   # (t + 1,)
    return pi, mu, Sigma, r, loglik

docs.title: Hidden Markov Models
docs.text:
A hidden Markov model describes a sequence of observations generated by a latent Markov chain. We will see an example of an HMM applied to part-of-speech tagging.

Notation. Let \(T\ge 1\) be the number of observation times. The complete data are \(X=(Y,Z)\).

  • \(Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T)\) is the hidden, time-homogeneous Markov chain. Each \(Z_t\) takes values in the state space \(\mathcal{S}\), with \(N_s=|S|\).
  • \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_T)\) is the observed sequence. Each \(Y_t\) takes one of \(N_o\) possible values. Given the entire state sequence \(Z=z\), the observations are conditionally independent, and the distribution of \(Y_t\) depends only on \(z_t\).

The HMM parameter is \(\boxed{\theta=(\pi,A,B)}\).

Parameter Meaning Entries \(\pi\) Initial distribution on \(S\) \(\pi_i=P(Z_1=i)\) \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{N_s\times N_s}\) One-step transition matrix \(a_{ij}=P(Z_{t+1}=j\mid Z_t=i)\) \(B=(b_{i\ell})\in\mathbb R^{N_s\times N_o}\) Observation generation matrix \(b_{i\ell}=P(Y_t=\ell\mid Z_t=i)\)

The pmf of the complete data, for a given choice of \(\theta\), is

\[ p_{\mathrm{cd}}(y,z\mid\theta) =\pi_{z_1}\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}a_{z_t z_{t+1}}\prod_{t=1}^{T}b_{z_t y_t}. \tag{27} \]

We consider the following three estimation tasks:

  1. Given the observed data \(y_{1: T}\) and \(\theta\), compute the conditional distribution of state \(z\).
  2. Given the observed data \(y_{1 : T}\) and \(\theta\), compute the most likely hidden state sequence \(z_{1: T}\).
  3. Given the observed data \(y_{1:T}\), compute the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\theta\).

docs.title: Posterior state probabilities and the forward-backward algorithm
docs.text:
In this section, we aim to provide an efficient way to compute

\[ P(Z_{t}=i \mid Y_{1}=y_{1}, \dots, Y_{T}=y_{T}, \theta) \tag{28} \]

and

\[ P(Z_{t}=i,Z_{t+1}=j\mid Y_{1}=y_{1},\dots,Y_{T}=y_{T},\theta). \tag{29} \]

For each \(i\in\mathcal S\) and \(1\le t\le T\), define the forward variable \(\alpha_i(t)\) and the backward variable \(\beta_i(t)\) by

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha_i(t)&\triangleq P(Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_t=y_t,Z_t=i\mid\theta),\\ \beta_i(t)&\triangleq P(Y_{t+1}=y_{t+1},\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid Z_t=i,\theta). \end{aligned} \tag{30} \]

At the endpoints, \(\alpha_i(1)=\pi_i b_{i y_1}\) and \(\beta_i(T)=1\). We leave the derivation of the recurrences for \(\alpha, \beta\) to the reader. Next, we see how \(\alpha, \beta\) help to find the two probabilities we want.

Note that

\[ \begin{aligned} P(Z_t=i,Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid\theta) &=P(Z_t=i,Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t}\mid\theta)\, P(Y_{t+1:T}=y_{t+1:T}\mid Z_t=i,Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t},\theta)\\ &=P(Z_t=i,Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t}\mid\theta)\, P(Y_{t+1:T}=y_{t+1:T}\mid Z_t=i,\theta)\\ &=\alpha_i(t)\,\beta_i(t). \end{aligned} \tag{31} \]

We can derive the conditional distribution of the state at time \(t\), given all the observations:

\[ \begin{aligned} \gamma_i(t)&\triangleq P(Z_t=i\mid Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T,\theta)\\ &=\frac{P(Z_t=i,Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid\theta)}{P(Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid\theta)}\\ &=\frac{\alpha_i(t)\beta_i(t)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}\alpha_j(t)\beta_j(t)}. \end{aligned} \tag{32} \]

From the above, for any \(i\) such that \(\gamma_{i}(t) > 0\),

\[ P(Y_{1}=y_{1},\dots,Y_{T}=y_{T}\mid \theta) = \frac{\alpha_{i}(t)\beta_{i}(t)}{\gamma_{i}(t)}. \tag{33} \]

Similarly,

\[ \begin{aligned} &P(Z_t=i,Z_{t+1}=j,Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid\theta)\\ &=P(Z_t=i,Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t}\mid\theta)\\ &\quad{}\cdot P(Z_{t+1}=j,Y_{t+1}=y_{t+1}\mid Z_t=i,Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t},\theta)\\ &\quad{}\cdot P(Y_{t+2:T}=y_{t+2:T}\mid Z_t=i,Z_{t+1}=j,Y_{1:t+1}=y_{1:t+1},\theta)\\ &=\alpha_i(t)\,a_{ij}\,b_{j y_{t+1}}\,\beta_j(t+1). \end{aligned} \tag{34} \]

From this, we derive the conditional distribution of a pair of states at consecutive times \(t\) and \(t+1\), given all observations:

\[ \begin{aligned} \xi_{ij}(t)&\triangleq P(Z_t=i,Z_{t+1}=j\mid Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T,\theta)\\ &=\frac{P(Z_t=i,Z_{t+1}=j,Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid\theta)} {P(Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\mid\theta)}\\ &=\frac{\alpha_i(t)a_{ij}b_{j y_{t+1}}\beta_j(t+1)} {\displaystyle\sum_{i',j'\in\mathcal S} \alpha_{i'}(t)a_{i'j'}b_{j' y_{t+1}}\beta_{j'}(t+1)}\\ &=\frac{\gamma_i(t)a_{ij}b_{j y_{t+1}}\beta_j(t+1)}{\beta_i(t)} \qquad\text{if }\beta_i(t)>0. \end{aligned} \tag{35} \]

where the final expression is derived using (33).

Algorithm (Forward-backward). Given the observations \(y_{1:T}\) and parameters \(\theta=(\pi,A,B)\), make two passes over the sequence.

  1. Forward pass. Initialize \(\alpha_i(1)=\pi_i b_{i y_1}\) for each \(i\in\mathcal S\). For \(t=1,\ldots,T-1\), compute

    \[ \alpha_j(t+1)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\alpha_i(t)a_{ij}b_{j y_{t+1}}. \tag{36} \]

  2. Backward pass. Initialize \(\beta_i(T)=1\) for each \(i\in\mathcal S\). For \(t=T,T-1,\ldots,2\), compute

    \[ \beta_i(t-1)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}a_{ij}b_{j y_t}\beta_j(t). \tag{37} \]

  3. Compute the posteriors.

    \[ \begin{align} P(Z_t=i\mid Y_{1:t}=y_{1:t},\theta) &=\frac{\alpha_i(t)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}\alpha_j(t)}, \tag{38}\\ \gamma_i(t)\triangleq P(Z_t=i\mid Y_{1:T}=y_{1:T},\theta) &=\frac{\alpha_i(t)\beta_i(t)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}\alpha_j(t)\beta_j(t)}. \tag{39} \end{align} \] \[ \begin{align} \xi_{ij}(t) &\triangleq P(Z_{t}=i,Z_{t+1}=j \mid Y_{1}=y_{1},\dots,Y_{T}=y_{T},\theta) \notag\\ &= \frac{\alpha_i(t)a_{ij}b_{j y_{t+1}}\beta_j(t+1)} {\displaystyle\sum_{u,v\in\mathcal S}\alpha_u(t)a_{uv}b_{v y_{t+1}}\beta_v(t+1)} \tag{40}\\ &= \frac{\gamma_{i}(t)a_{ij}b_{jy_{t+1}}\beta_{j}(t+1)}{\beta_{i}(t)}. \tag{41} \end{align} \]

docs.title: Most likely state sequence: Viterbi algorithm
docs.text:
Suppose the parameter \(\theta = (\pi, A, B)\) is known, and that \(Y = (Y_{1},\dots,Y_{T})\) is observed as \(y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T})\). We seek the MAP estimate \(\hat{Z}_{\text{MAP}}(y,\theta)\) of the entire state sequence \(Z=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T})\) given \(Y=y\).

\[ \hat{Z}_{\text{MAP}}(y,\theta)=\arg\max_{z} p_{Z|Y}(z|y,\theta)=\arg\max_{z}p_{\text{cd}}(y,z\mid \theta). \tag{42} \]

We use dynamic programming and define the variables

\[ \delta_{i}(t) \triangleq \max_{(z_{1},\dots,z_{(t-1)})} P(Z_{1}=z_{1},\dots,Z_{t-1}=z_{t-1},Z_{t}=i,Y_{1}=y_{1},\dots,Y_{t}=y_{t}\mid \theta). \tag{43} \]

We leave the derivation of the recurrence to the reader.

Algorithm (Viterbi). Compute the \(\delta\)'s and associated back pointers by a recursion forward in time:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{(initial condition)}\quad &\delta_i(1)=\pi(i)b_{i y_1}\\ \text{(recursive step)}\quad &\delta_j(t)=\max_i\{\delta_i(t-1)a_{ij}b_{j y_t}\}\\ \text{(storage of back pointers)}\quad &\phi_j(t)\triangleq\arg\max_i\{\delta_i(t-1)a_{ij}b_{j y_t}\}. \end{aligned} \tag{44} \]

Then \(z^* = \hat{Z}_{\text{MAP}}(y,\theta)\) satisfies \(p_{\text{cd}}(y, z^*\mid \theta)=\max_{i}\delta_{i}(T)\), and \(z^*\) is given by tracking backward in time:

\[ z_T^*=\arg\max_i \delta_i(T) \qquad\text{and}\qquad z_{t-1}^*=\phi_{z_t^*}(t)\quad\text{for }2\le t\le T. \tag{45} \]

docs.title: The Baum-Welch algorithm, or EM algorithm for HMMs
docs.text:
The parameter to be estimated is \(\theta = (\pi, A, B)\). The complete data consist of \((Y, Z)\), and the observed data are \(Y\). The initial parameter \(\theta^{(0)}=(\pi^{(0)}, A^{(0)}, B^{(0)})\) should have all entries strictly positive.

To compute \(Q(\theta \mid \theta^{(k)})\), taking logarithms in the expression (27) for the pmf of the complete data yields

\[ \log p_{\text{cd}}(y,z \mid \theta) = \log \pi_{z_{1}} + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \log a_{z_{t}z_{t+1}} + \sum_{t=1}^T \log b_{z_{t}y_{t}}. \tag{46} \]

Taking the expectation yields

\[ \begin{aligned} Q(\theta \mid \theta^{(k)}) &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \log p_{\text{cd}}(y, Z \mid \theta) \middle| y, \theta^{(k)} \right] \\ &= \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma_{i}(1) \log \pi_{i} + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \sum_{i,j \in \mathcal{S}} \xi_{ij}(t) \log a_{ij} \\ &\quad{}+ \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma_{i}(t) \log b_{i y_{t}}. \end{aligned} \tag{47} \]

where the variables \(\gamma_{i}(t)\) and \(\xi_{ij}(t)\) are defined using the model with parameter \(\theta^{(k)}\) according to (39) and (41).

Rewrite \(Q(\theta \mid \theta^{(k)})\) for easier optimization:

\[ \begin{aligned} Q(\theta \mid \theta^{(k)}) &= \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma_{i}(1) \log \pi_{i} \\ &\quad{}+ \sum_{i,j} \left( \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \xi_{ij}(t) \right) \log a_{ij} \\ &\quad{}+ \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{\ell \in \mathcal{O}} \left( \sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_{i}(t) \mathbf{1} \{y_{t} = \ell\} \right) \log b_{i\ell }. \end{aligned} \tag{48} \]

We skip the exact derivation. The maximization step of the EM algorithm gives:

\[ \begin{align} \pi_i^{(k+1)} &= \gamma_i(1), \tag{49}\\ a_{ij}^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\xi_{ij}(t)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\gamma_i(t)}, \tag{50}\\ b_{i\ell}^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_i(t)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{y_t=\ell\}}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_i(t)}. \tag{51} \end{align} \]

docs.title: Example: Part-of-speech tagging
docs.text:
Part-of-speech (POS) tagging assigns a grammatical category to each token in a sentence, using its context. In the lecture's sentence, raises is a verb and interest is a noun. In the HMM, \(Y_t\) is the observed word and \(Z_t\) is its tag.

Given a trained model, Viterbi finds the most likely tag sequence for a new sentence. An HMM can be trained on untagged text and then used to generate text.

docs.title: Supervised training
docs.text:
When every training word has a known tag, the maximum likelihood estimates are normalized counts. Let \(M\) be the number of sentences, and let \(\#\) count occurrences across the corpus. Count transitions only within a sentence.

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat\pi_i &=\frac{\#\{\text{sentences starting with tag }i\}}{M},\\ \hat a_{ij} &=\frac{\#\{\text{transitions }i\to j\}}{\#\{\text{transitions out of }i\}},\\ \hat b_{iw} &=\frac{\#\{\text{tokens with word }w\text{ and tag }i\}}{\#\{\text{tokens with tag }i\}}. \end{aligned} \tag{52} \]

docs.title: Unsupervised training
docs.text:
With only the words observed, the likelihood of a sentence sums over all possible tag sequences. For a sentence of length \(T\), the objective is

\[ \max_\theta \log p(y_{1:T}\mid\theta) =\max_\theta \log\sum_{z_{1:T}\in\mathcal S^T}p_{\mathrm{cd}}(y_{1:T},z_{1:T}\mid\theta). \tag{53} \]

For independent sentences, add their log likelihoods. The Baum-Welch algorithm is EM for this objective.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Bruce Hajek. Random Processes for Engineers. Cambridge University Press, 2015. Chapter 5, “Inference for Markov models.”
  • Kaare Brandt Petersen and Michael Syskind Pedersen. The Matrix Cookbook. Version: November 15, 2012. Section 2, “Derivatives.”
  • Tianxing He. Natural Language Processing, Part I. Lecture slides, Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences (IIIS), Tsinghua University.

docs.title: The term–document matrix
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal V=\{w_1,\ldots,w_m\}\) be the vocabulary and \(\mathcal D=\{d_1,\ldots,d_n\}\) be a collection of nonempty documents. The term–document (TD) matrix is \(W_{\mathrm{td}}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), with entries

\[ (W_{\mathrm{td}})_{ij}=c_{ij}, \qquad c_{ij}=\text{the number of occurrences of }w_i\text{ in }d_j. \]

Row \(i\) represents word \(w_i\) across the documents. Column \(j\) represents document \(d_j\) as a bag of words.

Three properties of raw counts motivate LSA.

  1. Direct overlap. The dot product between two word rows measures direct document overlap. If no document contains both words, their dot product is zero. For example, let \(e_1\) be cat paw and \(e_2\) be dog paw, with each listed word occurring once. The rows for cat and dog are \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), so their dot product is zero, even though the shared word paw links their contexts.
  2. Sparsity. Each word has one coordinate per document, and most words appear in only a small fraction of documents. The resulting word vectors are high-dimensional and mostly zero.
  3. Unequal weights. Long documents tend to have larger counts, and common words such as the can dominate a decomposition of the raw matrix, even though their presence does little to distinguish documents.

LSA uses TF-IDF to adjust the weights and truncated SVD to represent words and documents in a shared low-dimensional space.

docs.title: Singular value decomposition
docs.text:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), a singular value decomposition (SVD) is

\[ A=U\Sigma V^\top, \qquad U\in\mathbb R^{m\times m},\quad \Sigma\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}. \]

The matrices \(U\) and \(V\) are orthogonal. The only possibly nonzero entries of \(\Sigma\) are on its main diagonal. They are the singular values \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p\ge 0\), where \(p=\min(m,n)\).

Let \(r=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and let \(u_\ell\) and \(v_\ell\) be columns \(\ell\) of \(U\) and \(V\). Exactly \(r\) singular values are positive, so

\[ A=\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\sigma_\ell u_\ell v_\ell^\top =U_r\Sigma_rV_r^\top. \]

The factors have shapes \(m\times r\), \(r\times r\), and \(r\times n\), respectively. Every term in the sum is an \(m\times n\) rank-one matrix.

When \(A\) is a TD matrix, each row of \(U\) corresponds to a word. The rows of the full, square \(U\) are orthonormal, so using them as word vectors would give a cosine similarity of zero for every pair of distinct words.

docs.title: Best rank-\(k\) approximation
docs.text:
For \(1\le k\le r\), let \(U_k\) and \(V_k\) contain the first \(k\) columns of \(U\) and \(V\), and let \(\Sigma_k=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)\). The truncated SVD is

\[ A_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^\top =\sum_{\ell=1}^k\sigma_\ell u_\ell v_\ell^\top. \]

Theorem (Eckart–Young). The truncated SVD achieves the minimum squared Frobenius error among matrices of rank at most \(k\).

\[ \min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}} \|A-B\|_F^2 =\|A-A_k\|_F^2 =\sum_{\ell=k+1}^{r}\sigma_\ell^2, \qquad \|X\|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}^2. \]

Proof. Let \(P\) be the orthogonal projector onto the column space of any candidate \(B\) of rank at most \(k\). Since \((I-P)B=0\), the orthogonal decomposition of each column gives

\[ \|A-B\|_F^2 =\|P(A-B)\|_F^2+\|(I-P)A\|_F^2 \ge \|A\|_F^2-\|PA\|_F^2. \]

The orthogonality of the right singular vectors gives

\[ \|PA\|_F^2=\sum_{\ell=1}^r \sigma_\ell^2 a_\ell, \qquad a_\ell=\|Pu_\ell\|_2^2. \]

Each \(a_\ell\) lies in \([0,1]\), and \(\sum_{\ell=1}^r a_\ell\le\operatorname{tr}(P)\le k\). Allocating this weight to the \(k\) largest squared singular values gives the upper bound \(\|PA\|_F^2\le\sum_{\ell=1}^k\sigma_\ell^2\). Thus \(\|A-B\|_F^2\ge\sum_{\ell=k+1}^r\sigma_\ell^2\). The choice \(B=A_k\) attains this bound because the omitted rank-one terms are orthogonal in the Frobenius inner product. \(\square\)

docs.title: Latent word and document vectors
docs.text:
Let \(z_i=\bigl((U_k)_{i,:}\bigr)^\top\) be the \(k\)-dimensional word vector for \(w_i\), and let \(h_j=\Sigma_k\bigl((V_k)_{j,:}\bigr)^\top\) be the document vector for \(d_j\). The reconstruction is

\[ (A_k)_{ij}=z_i^\top h_j\approx A_{ij}. \]

If nonnegative association scores are desired, one can take \(\max\{z_i^\top h_j,0\}\). The Frobenius optimality theorem applies to the reconstruction before this clipping.

The columns of \(U_k\) remain orthonormal. Its rows can have nonzero inner products, so word vectors can reflect shared patterns across documents. The identity \(AV_k=U_k\Sigma_k\) shows how the original word rows are projected onto the retained directions.

Example (two documents). Return to the documents \(e_1=\) cat paw and \(e_2=\) dog paw introduced under direct overlap. With rows ordered as cat, dog, and paw, their TD matrix is

\[ W_{\mathrm{td}}= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Apply SVD to this raw count matrix to see the effect of truncation alone. Its leading right singular vector is \(v_1=(1,1)^\top/\sqrt{2}\). Projecting the cat and dog rows onto this direction gives both the coordinate \(1/\sqrt{2}\). The corresponding rows of \(U_1\) are equal as well, since the projection coordinates are divided by the same singular value. The shared occurrence of paw in \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) makes this common direction stronger than the direction that separates the documents.

docs.title: TF-IDF normalization
docs.text:
Let \(L_j\) be the number of tokens in document \(d_j\). The term frequency (TF) is the fraction of tokens in \(d_j\) that are instances of \(w_i\).

\[ \mathrm{TF}_{ij}=\frac{c_{ij}}{L_j}. \]

The document frequency is \(\mathrm{df}_i=|\{j:c_{ij}>0\}|\). The smoothed inverse document frequency (IDF) gives greater weight to words that occur in fewer documents.

\[ \mathrm{IDF}_i=1+\ln\!\left(\frac{n+1}{\mathrm{df}_i+1}\right). \]

Each document containing \(w_i\) contributes one to \(\mathrm{df}_i\), regardless of the number of occurrences. A word that appears in every document has \(\mathrm{IDF}_i=1\).

The TF-IDF weighted TD matrix \(A\) has entries

\[ A_{ij}=\mathrm{TF}_{ij}\,\mathrm{IDF}_i =\frac{c_{ij}\,\mathrm{IDF}_i}{L_j}. \]

Each occurrence of \(w_i\) contributes \(\mathrm{IDF}_i\) to the numerator. Dividing by \(L_j\) gives its average contribution per token in the document.

Example (seven documents). Consider seven documents \(d_1,\ldots,d_7\), represented as bags of words over the vocabulary \(\{\textit{cat},\textit{dog},\textit{the}\}\). Their complete word counts are:

Word \(d_1\) \(d_2\) \(d_3\) \(d_4\) \(d_5\) \(d_6\) \(d_7\) cat 1 1 0 0 0 0 0 dog 0 8 0 1 0 0 0 the 20 13 18 22 15 4 20 Document length 21 22 18 23 15 4 20

For instance, \(d_2\) contains one cat, eight dog tokens, and thirteen the tokens, for a total of 22 tokens. Both cat and dog occur in two documents, whereas the occurs in all seven.

The three word rows form the TD matrix; the document-length row records the column sums. The table gives \(n=7\), \(L_2=1+8+13=22\), \(\mathrm{df}_{\textit{cat}}=\mathrm{df}_{\textit{dog}}=2\), and \(\mathrm{df}_{\textit{the}}=7\). Substituting these counts into the TF and smoothed IDF formulas gives:

Word Count in \(d_2\) Document frequency TF IDF TF-IDF cat 1 2 \(1/22\) \(1+\ln(8/3)\approx 1.981\) \(0.090\) dog 8 2 \(8/22\) \(1+\ln(8/3)\approx 1.981\) \(0.720\) the 13 7 \(13/22\) \(1\) \(0.591\)

The weight of dog in \(d_2\) exceeds that of the because dog occurs in fewer documents.

docs.title: Full approach
docs.text:
1. Build the count matrix \(W_{\mathrm{td}}\) from the vocabulary and document collection.
  2. Compute TF-IDF to obtain the weighted matrix \(A\).
  3. Compute the leading \(k\) singular directions of \(A\) and form \(A_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^\top\).
  4. Use the rows of \(U_k\) as word embeddings and the columns of \(\Sigma_kV_k^\top\) as document embeddings. Word similarity can be measured by cosine similarity between nonzero word vectors. The dot product between a word vector and a document vector gives the corresponding reconstructed TF-IDF weight.
